titulo_es: Conditionals without if (inversion and conditional connectors)
descripcion_es: Had I known…, Should you need…, Were it not for…, provided that, unless, as long as, otherwise.
resumen: In formal register, if can be dropped by inverting should, were or had with the subject. There are also connectors that replace if, each with its own nuance: unless, provided that, as long as, on condition that, otherwise, but for.

filas: If you should need help, call me.
Should you need help, call me.
First conditional, remote and polite possibility
If I were in your position, I'd resign.
Were I in your position, I'd resign.
Second conditional
If it were not for your help, we'd fail.
Were it not for your help, we'd fail.
Second conditional meaning “if it weren't for” (es: de no ser por)
If we had known, we would have come.
Had we known, we would have come.
Third conditional
If it had not been for the rain, we'd have won.
Had it not been for the rain, we'd have won.
Third conditional meaning “if it hadn't been for” (es: de no haber sido por)

items: The negative is not contracted in the inversion: Had I not seen it (not “Hadn't I seen it”).
With verbs other than be in the second conditional, use were + to: Were the price to rise, sales would fall.
But for + noun is equivalent to were it not for / had it not been for: But for the storm, we would have arrived on time.

filas: unless
except if; if… not (es: a menos que, si no)
I won't go unless you come with me.
provided (that) / providing (that)
only if a condition is met (es: siempre que, con tal de que)
You can borrow it provided you return it tomorrow.
as long as / so long as
only if; on the condition that (es: mientras, siempre que)
As long as you're honest, I'll help you.
on condition that
only if a specific requirement is accepted (es: con la condición de que)
He agreed on condition that his name was not published.
otherwise
if not; or else (es: de lo contrario)
Hurry up; otherwise we'll miss the bus.
supposing / suppose
imagine that; what if…? (es: suponiendo que, ¿y si…?)
Supposing it rains, what will we do?
in case
as a precaution against something happening; not conditional (es: por si)
Take an umbrella in case it rains.

explicacion.texto: Careful: unless already contains the negative (= if… not), so it is not combined with another negative with the same meaning. And in case does not mean a conditional “in the event that” (Spanish “en caso de que”), but “just in case” (Spanish “por si acaso”): you take the precaution beforehand.

ejemplos.frase: Should you have any questions, please contact our office.
ejemplos.traduccion: Si tuviera alguna pregunta, póngase en contacto con nuestra oficina.

ejemplos.frase: Had I known about the strike, I would have taken the car.
ejemplos.traduccion: De haber sabido lo de la huelga, habría cogido el coche.

ejemplos.frase: Were it not for her patience, the project would have collapsed long ago.
ejemplos.traduccion: De no ser por su paciencia, el proyecto se habría venido abajo hace tiempo.

ejemplos.frase: You may keep the dog provided that you walk it every day.
ejemplos.traduccion: Puedes quedarte con el perro siempre que lo saques a pasear todos los días.

ejemplos.frase: Unless the weather improves, the match will be cancelled.
ejemplos.traduccion: A menos que mejore el tiempo, se suspenderá el partido.

ejemplos.frase: But for his quick reaction, there would have been an accident.
ejemplos.traduccion: De no ser por su rápida reacción, habría habido un accidente.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Hadn't I missed the train, I would have arrived on time.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Had I not missed the train, I would have arrived on time.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: In conditional inversion the negative is not contracted and goes after the subject.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I'll take a coat in case it will be cold.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I'll take a coat in case it is cold.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: After in case (and after unless, provided…) will is not used for the future.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Unless you don't hurry, you'll be late.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Unless you hurry, you'll be late.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Unless already means “if not”; adding another negative reverses the meaning.

ejercicios.frase: ___ you require further information, do not hesitate to contact us.
respuestas: Should
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the first row of the inversion table: Should + subject + base verb replaces if in a first conditional, with a nuance of remote and polite possibility. The clue is the verb require in the base form after the gap and the main clause in the imperative, typical of a business letter. Should you require is equivalent to If you require.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Should + subject replaces if in an open, polite conditional.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si necesita más información, no dude en ponerse en contacto con nosotros.

por_opcion.Should: Correct: Should you require is the polite inversion of the first conditional.
por_opcion.Would: Incorrect: would is not inverted to form conditionals; Would you require… would be a question.
por_opcion.Had: Incorrect: Had + subject needs a past participle (had you required) and is used for the third conditional, not for this open situation.
por_opcion.Unless: Incorrect: unless means “except if”; the sentence would tell them to get in touch if they do not need information.

ejercicios.frase: ___ I known you were ill, I would have visited you.
respuestas: Had
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the inversion of the third conditional in the table: Had + subject + past participle = If + subject + had + past participle. The clue is known, a past participle, and the main clause would have visited, typical of the third conditional. Had I known is equivalent to If I had known.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Third conditional without if: had + subject + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si hubiera sabido que estabas enfermo, te habría visitado.

por_opcion.Were: Incorrect: Were + subject goes with the second conditional and cannot be followed by known.
por_opcion.Had: Correct: Had I known is the inversion of the third conditional.
por_opcion.Should: Incorrect: Should + subject needs a base verb and is used for the first conditional.
por_opcion.If: Incorrect: “If I known” is not grammatical; with if you would need If I had known.

ejercicios.frase: You can stay out late ___ you phone us when you leave.
respuestas: as long as
ejercicios.explicacion: This is a connector from the table: as long as, meaning only if, which introduces the condition needed for the main clause to happen. The clue is the meaning: permission to come home late depends on phoning. After as long as, the present is used with future meaning (you phone).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: As long as introduces the condition that must be met (only if).
ejercicios.traduccion: Puedes volver tarde siempre que nos llames cuando salgas.

por_opcion.unless: Incorrect: it would say “you can come home late unless you phone us”, exactly the opposite.
por_opcion.as long as: Correct: as long as, meaning only if, introduces the condition for the permission.
por_opcion.in case: Incorrect: in case means “just in case”, a precaution; it does not express a condition.
por_opcion.otherwise: Incorrect: otherwise means “if not; or else” and goes between two independent clauses.

glosario.significado: volver tarde a casa, quedarse fuera hasta tarde

ejercicios.frase: Write the number down ___ you forget it.
respuestas: in case
ejercicios.explicacion: The sheet warns that in case is not conditional, but means “just in case”: you take the precaution before something happens. The clue is that writing the number down is a precaution against the possibility of forgetting it. After in case the present is used, without will.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In case expresses a precaution: “in case you forget”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Apunta el número por si se te olvida.

por_opcion.unless: Incorrect: “write it down unless you forget it” makes no sense.
por_opcion.provided: Incorrect: “write it down provided you forget it” reverses the logic of the precaution.
por_opcion.in case: Correct: in case expresses the precaution, in case you forget.
por_opcion.if: Incorrect: “write it down if you forget it” is illogical, because once you have forgotten it you can no longer write it down.

ejercicios.frase: ___ it not for the scholarship, she could not afford university.
respuestas: Were
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the row of the table Were it not for = If it were not for (es: de no ser por), in a second conditional. The clue is it not for after the gap and could not afford, a hypothetical result in the present. Were is inverted with the subject it and the negative goes after it, uncontracted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Were it not for = if it were not for (es: de no ser por), second conditional.
ejercicios.traduccion: De no ser por la beca, no podría pagarse la universidad.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Had
errores_previstos.explicacion: Had it not been for would be the third conditional (past) and would need been; here been is missing and the result is in the present.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Weren't
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the inversion the negative is not contracted: Were it not for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If
errores_previstos.explicacion: If it not for is not grammatical; with if you need the verb: If it were not for.

ejercicios.frase: We will not sign the contract ___ they lower the price.
respuestas: unless
until
ejercicios.explicacion: This is unless from the table of connectors: except if, equivalent to if… not. The clue is the negative in the main clause (will not sign) and the fact that the condition is lowering the price. Until is also correct and the sheet accepts it, although it changes the nuance to a time one. After both, the present is used with future meaning (they lower), without will.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Unless = if… not: we won't sign if they don't lower the price (until is also correct).
ejercicios.traduccion: No firmaremos el contrato a menos que bajen el precio (o: hasta que bajen el precio).

errores_previstos.respuesta: if
errores_previstos.explicacion: “We won't sign if they lower the price” says the opposite of what is intended.

errores_previstos.respuesta: unless not
errores_previstos.explicacion: Unless already contains the negative; adding another one reverses the meaning.

errores_previstos.respuesta: except
errores_previstos.explicacion: Except means “apart from” and goes with nouns; to introduce a conditional clause you use unless.

ejercicios.frase: Leave now; ___ you will get stuck in traffic.
respuestas: otherwise
ejercicios.explicacion: This is otherwise from the table of connectors: if not, if you don't do it. The clue is the semicolon, which separates two independent clauses: an order and the consequence of not following it. Otherwise links those two clauses; unless or if cannot be used like that, after a semicolon.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Otherwise = if not, if you don't do it.
ejercicios.traduccion: Sal ya; de lo contrario, te quedarás atascado en el tráfico.

errores_previstos.respuesta: unless
errores_previstos.explicacion: Unless introduces a subordinate condition, not a consequence after a semicolon.

errores_previstos.respuesta: if not
errores_previstos.explicacion: If not can be used in speech, but the single word the sentence needs is otherwise.

errores_previstos.respuesta: contrarily
errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal translation of Spanish “de lo contrario”; it is not a natural English connector here.

ejercicios.frase: ___ for the firefighters, the whole building would have burnt down.
respuestas: But
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the structure but for + noun from the list in the sheet, equivalent to had it not been for (es: de no haber sido por). The clue is for the firefighters (a noun, not a clause) and the result in the third conditional, would have burnt down. It is written with a capital letter because it comes at the start.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: But for + noun = if it hadn't been for.
ejercicios.traduccion: De no haber sido por los bomberos, todo el edificio se habría quemado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Except
errores_previstos.explicacion: Except for means “apart from”; it does not express the opposite condition.

errores_previstos.respuesta: If
errores_previstos.explicacion: If for the firefighters is not grammatical; with if you would need If it hadn't been for.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Without
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without the firefighters would be correct, but without for; with for after the gap, only But works.

glosario.significado: de no ser por, de no haber sido por

ejercicios.frase: If I were you, I would accept the offer.
respuestas: Were I you, I would accept the offer.
Were I you, I'd accept the offer.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the inversion of the second conditional in the table: Were + subject replaces If + subject + were. If I were you becomes Were I you, and the main clause does not change (would accept or I'd accept). It is a very formal form; in everyday speech If I were you is still preferred.
ejercicios.traduccion: Yo que tú, aceptaría la oferta.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Was I you, I would accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the inversion only were is possible, never was.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Were you I, I would accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The order of the pronouns is reversed; the formula is Were I you.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Should I be you, I would accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Should is for the first conditional; an unreal situation in the present needs were.

ejercicios.frase: If they had not helped us, we would have failed.
respuestas: Had they not helped us, we would have failed.
Had they not helped us, we'd have failed.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the inversion of the negative third conditional: Had + subject + not + past participle. The list in the sheet stresses that the negative is not contracted: Had they not helped, not Hadn't they helped. The main clause stays the same (would have failed or 'd have failed).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Negative third conditional: had + subject + not + past participle, without contraction.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si no nos hubieran ayudado, habríamos fracasado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Hadn't they helped us, we would have failed.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In the inversion the negative is not contracted and goes after the subject: Had they not.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Had not they helped us, we would have failed.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Not goes after the subject: Had they not helped.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Had they not help us, we would have failed.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After had comes the past participle: helped.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite without if, using inversion with should.
ejercicios.frase: If the flight is delayed, we will inform passengers by text.
respuestas: Should the flight be delayed, we will inform passengers by text.
Should the flight be delayed, we'll inform passengers by text.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the inversion of the first conditional with should: Should + subject + base verb. The form is delayed becomes be delayed, because should is followed by the infinitive without to. The main clause stays in the future (will inform or we'll inform). It is the typical formula of notices from airlines and companies.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Should + subject + base verb (be) replaces if + present.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si el vuelo se retrasa, informaremos a los pasajeros por SMS.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Should the flight is delayed, we will inform passengers by text.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After should comes the base verb: be delayed.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Should the flight be delayed, we would inform passengers by text.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Inversion with should does not change the main clause: it is still will inform.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Should be the flight delayed, we will inform passengers by text.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject goes right after should: Should the flight be delayed.

ejercicios.frase: Hadn't she called, we would have waited all night.
respuestas: Had she not called, we would have waited all night.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the typical mistake mentioned in the sheet: in conditional inversion the negative is not contracted and goes after the subject. Hadn't she called looks like a negative question, not a condition. The correct form is Had she not called; the main clause stays the same.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In the inversion, the negative is not contracted: had she not.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si ella no hubiera llamado, habríamos esperado toda la noche.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Hadn't she called, we would have waited all night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: the negative is not contracted in the inversion.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Had not she called, we would have waited all night.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Not goes after the subject: Had she not.

ejercicios.frase: I'll lend you the car provided that you will drive carefully.
respuestas: I'll lend you the car provided that you drive carefully.
I will lend you the car provided that you drive carefully.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is provided that from the table of connectors: only if a condition is met. The sheet points out that after conditional connectors will is not used for the future; instead, the present is used with future meaning, as after if. So will drive becomes drive. The main clause can be contracted (I'll) or full (I will).
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After provided that, use the present with future meaning, not will.
ejercicios.traduccion: Te dejaré el coche siempre que conduzcas con cuidado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll lend you the car provided that you will drive carefully.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: will does not go after provided that.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll lend you the car provided that you would drive carefully.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Would does not go after the connector either; use the present drive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll lend you the car provided that you drives carefully.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With you the present takes no -s.

respuestas: Should you change your mind let me know
Let me know should you change your mind
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the inversion of the first conditional with should: Should + subject + base verb, followed by the main clause in the imperative. The order is Should you change your mind (condition) + let me know (main clause). Change your mind is a fixed collocation: to change your opinion. As in any conditional, the main clause can come first: Let me know should you change your mind is also correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Should + subject + base verb; the main clause can go before or after.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Should change you your mind let me know
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject you goes right after should, before the verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You should change your mind let me know
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without inversion, you should change your mind means “you ought to change your opinion”; it is not a condition. To replace if, should goes before the subject.

respuestas: Were the government to raise taxes consumption would fall
ejercicios.explicacion: The list in the sheet points out that, with verbs other than be, the inverted second conditional is formed with Were + subject + to + infinitive. Here: Were the government to raise taxes = If the government raised taxes. The main clause goes with would + infinitive (consumption would fall). It is a very formal structure, frequent in economic analysis.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Were + subject + to + infinitive for a second conditional with a verb other than be.
ejercicios.traduccion: Si el Gobierno subiera los impuestos, el consumo caería.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Were the government raise to taxes consumption would fall
errores_previstos.explicacion: To goes before the infinitive: to raise.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The government were to raise taxes consumption would fall
errores_previstos.explicacion: Without inversion the if is missing; the condition must start with Were.

descripcion_larga_es: In formal English, if can disappear if the subject is inverted with should, were or had (Should you need help…, Had we known…). In addition, connectors such as unless, provided that, as long as, otherwise or but for replace if, each with its own nuance. It is a typical feature of written, business and legal register. Spanish speakers find it difficult because Spanish has no such inversion and because they translate in case as “en caso de que”.

contexto.que_es: These are two ways of expressing conditions without if. The first is inversion: should + subject + base verb (polite first conditional), were + subject (second) and had + subject + past participle (third), with the negative uncontracted. The second is conditional connectors with a nuance: unless (except if), provided that and as long as (only if), otherwise (if not), but for (if it weren't for).
contexto.por_que_importa: Inversion is very frequent in formal correspondence, contracts and institutional texts (Should you have any questions…), and using it well shows a visible C1 level in a written exam. Connectors change the meaning: confusing unless with if, or in case with Spanish “en caso de que”, can say the opposite of what you mean.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In formal letters and emails, in reports, in contract clauses and in speeches. The signals are an auxiliary at the start of a clause that is not a question (Had I…, Were it not…), and conditional connectors. Spanish speakers tend to contract the negative (Hadn't I…), to add another negative after unless and to put will after provided or in case.
